studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Let Hope Divert Them
studies.meaning: After the letters and a statement about the Book comes a prediction. Those refusing now will wish they had submitted. Early scholars place that wish at death or at the reckoning, and the sources keep both. Then an instruction that sounds like release but is not. The messenger is told to leave them to eating, enjoyment and being diverted by long expectation. The final verse gives the reason the instruction is safe to follow. No town was ever removed without a written term already set for it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, opening a surah that will move quickly to the making of the human being and the refusal of Iblis. The audience was prosperous, and the message threatened arrangements that were working. Nothing here reports an occasion. The instruction to leave them alone belongs to a stage where argument had been offered repeatedly and was no longer producing anything new.

keyTerms.note: A particle that grammarians read either as rarely or as often, and both readings are recorded. It occurs in only this one place in the whole Quran. That is why its force is discussed at such length.
Hope stretched over distance, the assumption that there will be time later. The definite form appears once in the Quran, here. The classical tradition habitually sets it against the appointed term.
A written and known decree. The phrase occurs only here. Naming it as written removes any suggestion of improvisation, so the delay a person reads as safety is a term already fixed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Long-range planning was how Meccan wealth was built. A merchant committed capital to a caravan that would not return for months. He arranged marriages years ahead and thought in seasons rather than days. That habit of mind is exactly what this passage names. Expectation of future time was not a weakness in that culture. It was the skill the whole economy ran on.
studies.didYouKnow: Three of the phrases in these opening verses occur nowhere else in the Quran. The particle in the second verse appears only here. The definite word for long expectation appears only here. The phrase for a known writ appears only here. Very few passages of this length hold that many terms unique to themselves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies distraction rather than argument as the real obstacle. Eating, enjoying and assuming there is time are not crimes, and none of them is named as one. Together, though, they postpone the question indefinitely. Placing a written term behind the whole scene also changes what patience means for the one watching. Nothing is running late, because the schedule was never his to read.

crossReferences.why: Names the same distraction, abundance occupying people until they reach the graves.
States the fixed term for every nation, unable to be advanced or delayed by an hour.
Uses the only other occurrence of this word for hope, attaching it to lasting good deeds instead.

studies.applyIt: Notice the phrase later this year in your own thinking. It covers the conversation you will have, the change you will make, the person you will visit. Pick the one that has been postponed longest. Put a date on it in your calendar today. Long expectation is what this passage names. A date is its opposite.
studies.explainEasier: One day the people who say no will wish they had listened. For now they eat, enjoy themselves, and think there is always more time. But every town has a set day written down.

studies.title: We Send Them Only With Truth
studies.meaning: A rule about terms is followed by two quoted taunts and one short answer. No community outruns or delays its appointed span. Then the objectors call the man given the reminder mad, and demand that angels be brought if he is truthful. The reply refuses the request by explaining what angels are for. They descend only with the settled matter, and once they do, no further waiting is granted. Early scholars read this as saying the demand asks for the end of the reprieve rather than for evidence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Demands for a visible angel are recorded in several surahs from this period. Sometimes the request was for a warner to come alongside the messenger. Calling a man mad was the standard charge against anyone who claimed to hear from the unseen. In that culture, being seized by a spirit was the ready way to explain such speech.

keyTerms.note: The word for remembrance and for what prompts it, used here by the objectors themselves for what was sent down. Even in mockery they name the message accurately, which is part of the passage's irony.
Built on the same root as the word for the unseen beings called jinn. So the accusation is literally that he is jinn-touched. It explains unusual speech by assigning it to an unseen source.
From the verb for looking and waiting, in a form meaning granted time. The same word appears later in this surah, when Iblis asks for exactly this and receives it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had a recognised category for people who spoke from an unseen source. Soothsayers delivered rhymed oracles and were understood to have a jinn companion feeding them. They were consulted and paid without being trusted. Calling a man possessed was therefore not merely an insult. It placed him in a known professional slot, one his audience already knew how to discount.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran answers the demand for angels in several places, with a different reason each time. One passage says that if an angel had come down, the matter would have been settled with no reprieve. Another says an angel sent to people would have had to be made a man, leaving everyone as confused as before. A third says angels are sent to those who live where the messenger lives.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer treats the reprieve itself as the mercy being overlooked. Angels descending in the requested form would end the interval in which anyone can still change position. Granting the demand would cost the demanders everything. That turns an unanswered request into a form of protection. It also says something about how the unseen works. It does not appear on request, and its appearance would mean the matter is closed.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same demand, saying the matter would have been settled and no respite given.
Records the same request and describes what seeing the angels will actually mean for sinners.
Uses the same word for respite later in this surah, when Iblis asks for it and is granted it.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have asked for that you are glad you did not receive on your own timetable. A job, a relationship, a confrontation. Notice that the delay was doing something. Then name one thing you are pressing for now, and consider what the interval before it might be for.
studies.explainEasier: They said the man with the message was mad. They told him to bring angels if he was telling the truth. The answer is that angels only come when it is all over. Then no one gets more time.

studies.title: The Reminder And Its Keeper
studies.meaning: The famous first line uses forms of emphasis three times over. We, and only We, sent down the Reminder, and We are its guardians. Early scholars divide over how far the pledge reaches. Most read it of the Quran and its keeping, safe from loss or change. Some stretch it to cover the message and the one who carries it. The four ayat that follow say why such a pledge is needed. Mocking a messenger is set out as a pattern, not an accident.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Three ayat before this passage, opponents are quoted calling the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) mad and demanding angels as proof. The pledge to keep the text lands in the middle of that mockery. The believers were few. The revealed words lived mainly in memory and on scattered scraps. No particular occasion is reported. The surah takes its name from a rock-cut settlement mentioned later in it.

keyTerms.note: One of the Quran's names for itself, from the root for remembering and mentioning. Calling revelation a reminder implies the content is not new information but something the hearer already owes.

A plural participle of guarding, used of watchmen, memorisers and anything kept intact. The same root gives the title for someone who holds the whole text in memory, which is one way the pledge has been carried.

A word for a beaten track that later travellers follow. Here it names the established pattern of how earlier peoples behaved and what happened to them, which is presented as evidence rather than as threat.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Texts in that world were fragile things. People wrote on bone, palm stalks, thin stone and scraps of leather. One fire or flood could take a whole library. What held a poem whole for a century was not parchment but a trained memory. Reciters carried thousands of lines and were corrected in public if they slipped. A promise to keep a text safe was a promise about people as much as about materials.
studies.didYouKnow: The pledge is given in the royal we and repeated in the same breath. Arabic uses that doubling for oaths. The wording does not say the Reminder will not be attacked. It says it will be guarded. That is a claim about the outcome, not about ease. The surah later mentions a valley whose rock-cut tombs still stand in northern Arabia.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage ties the survival of the text to God, not to the believers. That changes what keeping it safe means. It is not put forward as a feat of scholarship or of memory, though both are how it happened. It is put forward as something taken on from the other side. That caps the worry about whether the Quran is intact. It also caps the credit. And the ayat that follow refuse to read rejection as a sign the message failed.

crossReferences.why: Says falsehood cannot approach the Book from any side, the same guarantee stated negatively.
Assigns the gathering and the reciting of the revelation to God, not to its receiver.
States the same pattern of mockery: no messenger came without being ridiculed.

studies.applyIt: Learn three ayat by heart this month. Not a whole surah, and not because memorising earns anything: choose three you already half know and get them exact, in order, without looking. The pledge in this passage has been kept through ordinary people doing precisely that. You will also find you notice them in recitation for the rest of your life.
studies.explainEasier: God says that he sent down this message himself, and that he will keep it safe. People laughed at every messenger who came before. That has always been the pattern.

studies.title: A Gateway In The Sky
studies.meaning: The most extreme sign imaginable is granted as a supposition. A door opens in the sky and they climb through it. The passage gives their reaction: our eyes are being blocked, in fact we have been bewitched. Early scholars note that both halves of that reply are explanations. The second is stronger than the first, since it dismisses not one perception but the whole faculty. The following verses then describe the sky itself as set with constellations and guarded. That is the standing arrangement they would have been passing through.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the objectors' demand for angels and the statement that earlier peoples mocked their messengers too. The audience had asked for specific signs, and other surahs list them. There was a spring made to gush, a house of gold, an ascent into the sky. This passage takes the largest of those requests and answers it before it is granted.

keyTerms.note: The verb for going up by degrees, sharing a root with the word for a stairway. It describes a gradual climb rather than a sudden vision. So they are given all the time they could want.
The early Arabic dictionary writers give both dammed up, as water is stopped, and made intoxicated. Either way the claim is that the instrument has failed, which is what the objection needs to work.

The word also means fortified towers, and both senses were current. Placed beside the guarding described next, the fortress sense turns the sky into a structure with defences rather than an open expanse.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Soothsayers in Arabia claimed access to news from above. The culture had a working account of how it arrived: something listened at the edge of the unseen and passed fragments down. The shooting stars everyone saw at night were part of that picture. When this passage speaks of a guarded sky and a pursuing flame, it is engaging a picture of the world its audience already held.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran presses this argument in several forms. One passage says a book on parchment they could touch with their hands would still have been called plain magic. Another says that even seeing lumps of the sky fall, they would call it a mass of clouds. In each case a sense is granted and then dismissed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a move that no evidence can survive. It is doubting the instrument rather than the thing seen. Once perception itself is suspect, every possible sign has an answer waiting, and the argument cannot be tested from the inside. That is why the surah stops asking for belief on evidence after this point. What follows instead is a description of the world as it actually is, offered to whoever will take it.

crossReferences.why: Says a book they could touch with their hands would still have been called plain magic.
Has them explain away falling pieces of the sky as nothing more than gathered clouds.
States the same conclusion, that every sign coming would not move those already settled.

studies.applyIt: Notice the last time you dismissed something by questioning the source rather than the claim. The study was funded by someone, the person had a motive, the account was biased. Sometimes that is exactly right. Try separating the two questions once this week, and answer the claim on its own, whatever you conclude about the source.
studies.explainEasier: Even if a door opened in the sky and they walked up through it, they would not believe. They would say their eyes were tricked. God has set the sky with stars and keeps it guarded.

studies.title: All Things In Measure
studies.meaning: Attention moves from the guarded sky down to the ground in one step. The earth is spread out, and weights are set into it. Everything growing there is described as measured out. Then livelihoods are named. The sentence adds a group easy to miss: creatures for whom you are not the providers. Early scholars take this as covering dependants and animals alike, everything living off an arrangement nobody present set up. The passage lists provision as part of the structure rather than as a separate favour.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the objectors are shown explaining away a gateway in the sky. The surah turns from what they will not accept to what is already in front of them. This move from sky to earth to sustenance recurs across the Quran. Here it introduces a longer passage about stores, winds and water.

keyTerms.note: The verb for extending something, as a cloth is unrolled or a rope drawn out. It describes the earth as it is met by someone standing on it. That is how the Quran usually speaks of the ground.
From the root for a ship riding at anchor. The word does not mean mountain but something that holds steady. So the image is of weights set to keep a spread surface from shifting.
A passive form from the verb to weigh on a balance. It says what grows was measured before it appeared. That makes the vegetation itself the record of a calculation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Weighing was the daily business of a market town. Grain, dates, silver and incense all moved by balance. A merchant's honesty was judged by his weights, which were checked and sometimes disputed in public. Describing what grows from the ground as weighed out borrowed the most trusted instrument in Mecca. It applied that instrument to something no one had thought of measuring.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran repeatedly names creatures that carry no provision of their own and are fed nonetheless. One passage says that many a creature does not carry its sustenance, and that God provides for them and for you. Another states that there is no moving creature on earth whose sustenance is not upon God. It adds that He knows where it lives and where it rests.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Provision is presented as part of the design rather than as charity added afterwards. The earth is spread, steadied and planted in measure, and livelihoods are simply the next item on the same list. That has a consequence for how a person reads their own supply. It arrives through an arrangement that came before them. Naming those they do not provide for extends the point past the household, since the same structure feeds what nobody is responsible for.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same sequence, the earth spread with mountains and rivers, as signs for those who reflect.
Names creatures that carry no provision, and says God provides for them and for you alike.
States that no moving creature's sustenance is anywhere but with God, recorded in a clear book.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing you will eat today and trace it back three steps: who moved it, who grew it, what weather it needed. Stop when you reach something nobody arranged. The ayah puts provision inside the structure of the world rather than beside it. Tracing a single item is the shortest way to feel that.
studies.explainEasier: God spread out the earth and set mountains in it to hold it steady. Everything that grows there is measured. He gives food to you, and to living things you do not feed at all.

studies.title: The Storehouses Of Everything
studies.meaning: Two claims about supply. Everything that exists has its stores with God. What comes down arrives in a known measure, so scarcity and abundance are both quantities rather than accidents. Then the mechanism: winds are sent that make things fertile, water falls, you are given it to drink. The closing clause is the sting. You are not the ones who store it. Early scholars note the ayah gives people the drinking and withholds the keeping. That is exactly the division everyone experiences and rarely states.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage moving from the sky to the earth to what sustains life on it. Mecca had no river and no farmland, and its water came from wells in a dry valley. An audience in that setting did not need the point about storage explained. Nobody there had ever held a reserve of rain. The whole city's water security rested on sources they had not made.

keyTerms.note: Plural of the room where valuables are kept under lock. Saying every single thing has such a store with God turns supply into something released rather than something that happens to appear.
From the root for measuring and for power. It states that quantity is decided rather than accidental. That applies as much to a year of little rain as to a year of much.
The word occurs once in the Quran. It is used of winds that carry what makes things bear, and the early scholars connect it to the pollination of palms and to clouds made heavy with water.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Date palms had to be pollinated by hand or by wind. Every farmer in the oases knew the season for it and what a failure cost. Water itself could not be hoarded in a hot valley. Skins leaked, cisterns evaporated, and wells were shared under agreements that took generations to settle. A Meccan household lived on a supply it could use but never accumulate.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for winds that make things bear appears only once in the whole Quran. The Quran describes winds elsewhere in the same role without this term. It says that God sends the winds which stir clouds and drive them to dead ground, reviving it. Only this passage names the winds themselves by a word taken from fertility.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things people find hard to hold together are stated in one breath. Supply is unlimited at the source, since everything has its stores. It is strictly measured at delivery. That rules out both the anxiety that there is not enough and the assumption that more is always available. Denying human beings the role of storekeeper then removes the last illusion of control, since what can be drunk today cannot be secured for a decade.

crossReferences.why: States the same authority over supply, spreading bounty for some and reducing it for others.
Asks who sent down the water you drink, and notes it could have been made undrinkable.
Describes the winds driving clouds to dead land and uses the reviving as an image of resurrection.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you try to stockpile against the future. Money is obvious; more often it is energy, goodwill, or a sense of being ahead. Ask honestly how much of it actually keeps. The ayah grants you the drinking and denies you the storing, and most of what we hoard turns out to work the same way.
studies.explainEasier: God has a store of everything, and he sends it down in a set amount. He sends winds and rain so you have water to drink. You could never store that water yourselves.

studies.title: And We Are The Inheritors
studies.meaning: Giving life and causing death are stated together, and then a title is added that reframes both. We are the ones who remain. Early scholars explain the inheritance as what happens when every owner has gone and everything reverts. The next verse says those who go ahead and those who lag behind are equally known. The classical readings take that variously as earlier and later generations, or as those first and last in ranks and in obedience. Then the gathering, and then the clay.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage that has moved from the guarded sky through the earth and its provision to the human being. The surah is building its case from structure rather than from argument at this stage. No occasion is reported. The audience accepted a creator and disputed the gathering. That is why these four verses put creation and resurrection inside a single sequence.

keyTerms.note: The word for those who receive what an owner leaves. Used of God it means what stays when everything else has gone. So the term describes permanence through the vocabulary of succession.
Occurring once in the Quran, paired here with its opposite. The classical readings run from earlier and later generations to those forward and behind in rank, and the sources keep the range.
Clay dried to the point where it rings when struck. The word appears four times in the Quran, three of them in this surah. It names a material both fragile and resonant.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fights over inheritance were among the bitterest things an Arabian clan handled. Herds, wells and standing were divided when a man died. The arguments could run for years and change a family for good. Everyone knew that what you own is temporary. Everything passes to someone else in the end. This passage takes that and asks who is at the end of the chain.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for clay dried until it rings appears four times in the Quran. Three of those are in this surah, in verses twenty-six, twenty-eight and thirty-three. The third is spoken by Iblis. He repeats the description of the material back to God as his reason for refusing. It is used as a boast about material and as an insult about it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming God as the one who remains puts every possession into a chain that has an end. That is a claim about time rather than about ownership. Things are not merely lent; they are on their way somewhere. Setting this beside the knowledge of who goes ahead and who lags behind also removes the anonymity of a crowd. Whatever the gathering is, it is not a mass event. Each position is already known.

crossReferences.why: States the same inheritance directly, of the earth and everyone on it, with the return to Him.
Puts the same idea as a contrast, everyone upon it perishing while the face of your Lord remains.
Traces the making of the human being from clay through its stages to a new creature.

studies.applyIt: Pick up something in your home you would be sorry to lose, and ask who will have it in eighty years. Not to make yourself gloomy; simply to place the object correctly. The ayah does not ask you to stop caring for what you own. It asks you to know where in the chain you are standing.
studies.explainEasier: God gives life and God brings death. In the end everything is left to him. He knows who came first and who came later. He will gather them all together.

studies.title: Formed, Then Breathed Into
studies.meaning: Two materials are named before anything happens. The unseen beings were made earlier from a scorching fire. The human being was made from dried clay out of dark mud. Then comes the announcement to the angels and the condition attached. When I have shaped him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him. Early scholars are careful that the breathing is not a division of God's own being but an honour given. They note that the command follows the breath rather than the clay.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This scene appears in several surahs with different portions preserved, and the Quran assumes the outline is known. Here it is placed after a long passage on the sky, the earth and provision. So the making of the human being arrives as the last item in a description of how things are, rather than as a separate story.

keyTerms.note: The second word names a searing wind that gets into the pores. The compound describes fire at its most invasive rather than its brightest. That is the material assigned to the unseen beings.
The first word is black mud that has stood. The second means either poured into a mould or altered by time. Both senses are recorded. Either way the material has a history before the shaping.
The possessive marks honour rather than composition, as the Quran elsewhere calls a house My house. Early scholars hold that nothing of God's essence is divided or transferred by the phrase.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Potters worked with exactly this sequence, and everyone had watched it. River mud was gathered and left to stand until it darkened and grew workable. It was shaped by hand, then dried until it rang under a knuckle. A vessel at that stage was finished in form and still useless. The account borrows a craft its audience knew intimately and stops the process one step before the end.
studies.didYouKnow: This scene is told in at least six surahs, and each keeps different details. One records the angels asking why a creature who would shed blood should be placed on earth, and the teaching of the names. Another gives the material as clay without the mud. This surah is the only one that names the material three separate times in eight verses.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Honour is located in what was added rather than in the material. That is the point Iblis will miss in the next verses. Clay is not dignified and the passage does not pretend otherwise. The command to bow comes only after the breathing. That sets a pattern for how the Quran speaks about human worth throughout, as something given rather than owned. It explains why an argument from material misses the case entirely.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same sequence, forming, breathing and the command, and then the refusal and its reason.
Preserves the angels' question about a creature who would shed blood, and the teaching of the names.
Joins the same breathing to the giving of hearing, sight and understanding, and to thankfulness.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you find it hard to respect, and separate the two questions this passage separates. One is what they are made of, in behaviour and circumstance. The other is what was put into them that had nothing to do with any of that. You do not have to like them. Just notice which of the two your judgement is resting on.
studies.explainEasier: God made the jinn out of a burning fire. He made the first man out of dried clay from dark mud. Then he breathed his own spirit into him, and told the angels to bow down to him.

studies.title: He Refused To Be Among Them
studies.meaning: Everyone bowed, and the exception is stated twice over. He refused, and he would not be among those bowing. The question put to him is about company rather than obedience, asking what kept him from being with them. His answer repeats the material description word for word from the announcement. Early scholars read that as an argument from substance: he will not bow to something made of that. The reply names the consequence without arguing back.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah addressed to a people whose objection to the message was also partly about rank. Their complaint was that revelation had come to an ordinary man from among them. That is an argument about material in a different form. The scene is told across several surahs. This version keeps the exchange short and gives most of its space to the refusal itself.

keyTerms.note: A blunt verb of refusal with no explanation attached. Placing it before any reasoning shows the position was taken first. The argument about clay arrives afterwards as its justification.
A participle naming a group rather than an act, and the question asks why he was not among them. What is being refused is described as membership. That is a different failure from disobedience.
From the root for stoning or pelting something away. It names expulsion by force rather than a title. The same word described the devils repelled from the sky earlier in this surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Precedence was visible and constantly negotiated in Arabian gatherings. Where a man sat, when he spoke, and whether he rose for someone were public statements about rank. Refusing an expected courtesy was a serious act done in front of witnesses. The scene here would have read as that kind of moment. It was not a private disagreement but a refusal made in an assembly where everyone else complied.
studies.didYouKnow: The refusal is reported in several surahs, and the stated reason is consistent wherever it is given. I am better than he: You created me from fire and him from clay. In this surah the reason is phrased differently. It repeats back the exact description of the material used in the announcement. The objection quotes the very words it is answering.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Pride is diagnosed as a comparison of origins. The refusal is not a denial of God's authority, since the speaker addresses God directly throughout and never disputes His right to command. What is disputed is the worth of the one being honoured, judged by what he is made of. That is why the passage placed the breathing before the command. The case for honour was never the clay. So the argument about clay was never an answer.

crossReferences.why: Gives the reason in its usual form, better than he, created from fire against mud.
Adds God's question about whether he was too proud, and the same answer about the two materials.
Records the refusal as a question, whether he should bow to one created from mud.

studies.applyIt: Notice one person you would find it hard to take instruction from because of what they are rather than what they said. Younger, less qualified, from somewhere you rate lower. Take one piece of their advice this week on its own merits. The argument from material is the oldest one there is, and it is usually still doing its work quietly.
studies.explainEasier: All the angels bowed down. Iblis would not join them. He said he would not bow to a man made out of dried clay. God told him to get out.

studies.title: Until The Appointed Time
studies.meaning: A curse is pronounced until the Day of Recompense, and then something unexpected happens. The one expelled makes a request, and it is granted. Early scholars note the exact wording of both sides. He asks for time until the day people are raised. The answer gives him time until the day of the known appointment, which is not quite the same phrase. The sources discuss the difference at length without settling it. What is not in doubt is that a request from an enemy was answered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the middle of the scene that follows the making of the human being. The exchange appears in several surahs with slight variations in the wording of the request and the grant. Its placement here matters. This surah has just told its audience that no community is destroyed except at its written term, and the reprieve granted here belongs to the same principle.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to drive away and exclude. It names removal from mercy rather than a curse spoken aloud. That is why it can be stated as a fact with a stated duration.
From the verb for looking, in a form meaning to give someone a period before acting. It is the standard word for extending a debtor's term. So the request uses ordinary commercial language.
A moment fixed and known, though known to whom is left open. Early scholars note that the answer does not simply repeat the request's wording. They preserve the question rather than resolving it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Giving someone more time was a familiar deal. A lender could grant a debtor more time. The extra time was always stated with an end date. A delay with no end was no deal at all. Everyone knew that extra time is not a pardon. The words of this exchange come straight out of that practice. They include the asking and the bounded answer.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran records this exchange in at least three surahs. In two of them the request is for respite until the day people are raised. The answer grants respite until the day of the known time, using a phrase that does not repeat the request. Classical scholars noticed the mismatch. They discussed whether the two days are the same, without reaching a common answer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A request from an enemy in open revolt is granted. That says something hard and important about how the world is arranged. The stretch that follows is the whole of human history. It exists by permission, not by an oversight. Its limit matters too. Everything that happens in this stretch happens inside a term. That term was set at the start, and it is known at least to the one who set it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same expulsion and the same request and grant, in almost identical wording.
Records the request and the answer with the same phrase about the day of the known time.
States earlier in this surah that no community outruns or delays its own appointed term.

studies.applyIt: Consider that the time you are living in is described here as a granted interval rather than a default state. Not to frighten yourself. Simply pick one thing today that you would do differently if you took that literally, and do that one thing. The passage treats the whole stretch as an extension with a term attached.
studies.explainEasier: God told Iblis to leave, and said he would be cursed until the Day of Judgement. Iblis asked for more time until people are raised. God gave him time, but only until a day God has fixed.

studies.title: I Will Make It Look Good
studies.meaning: The stated method is not force, and it is not lying about facts. It is making things on earth look attractive. Early scholars note how modest a power that describes. Nothing is created, nothing is compelled, and no new option is introduced. The surface of what is already there is adjusted. The oath that follows extends the claim to everyone. The passage lets it stand unchallenged for one verse, before the exception arrives.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the reprieve is granted. The surah has just spent several verses describing a world made in measure and provided for. This declaration follows directly. Its placement suggests the danger is not a rival creation but a twisted view of the one that exists. The surah develops that as it goes on.

keyTerms.note: From a root for losing the way and for a mind gone wrong. The speaker puts his own refusal on God. Early scholars note this as the first move of a position that will not examine itself.
An intensive verb for adorning something, sharing a root with the word for finery. The work described is cosmetic. It is applied to the appearance of things rather than to the things themselves.
The stated arena, and it is a limit as much as a scope. Nothing is claimed beyond this world. So the whole enterprise is confined to the interval that was just granted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Traders knew the difference between goods and the way goods are shown. Dates were arranged with the best fruit on top. Cloth was shown in a particular light. A camel could be walked in a way that hid a fault for as long as the buyer was watching. Nobody in that market thought the display changed the goods. They knew it changed the sale.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses this word for making deeds look attractive in many places, and it does not always name the same agent. Several passages give the beautifying to Satan. One gives it to God, as how things are left to seem. One asks about the man whose evil deed was made to look good, so that he thinks it good. The verb stays the same while the framing shifts.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The power claimed here is remarkably limited, and therefore worth taking seriously. Nothing is added to the world. Nothing is taken from the person's ability to choose. What changes is how something looks at the moment of deciding. That places the whole struggle inside perception, which is why the Quran keeps returning to attention and reflection. The blaming of God in the first clause also stands as a warning about how such a position keeps itself going.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same beautifying at work in a specific battle, followed by immediate abandonment.
Asks about the man whose evil deed was made attractive so that he considers it good.
Joins the hardening of hearts to deeds made to appear good, when calamity failed to humble them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision you made that felt obviously right at the time and looked different a week later. Nothing changed except the framing. Before your next big choice, write one sentence describing it in the plainest words you can find, with no reasons attached. That single move undoes most of what this verse describes.
studies.explainEasier: Satan says he will make wrong things on earth look good to people. He cannot force anyone. He can only change how things look. He says he will do this to everyone.

studies.title: Over My Servants, No Authority
studies.meaning: An exception is carved out of a total claim, and one word is worth noticing. In the grammar of the sentence it names people who have been made pure, not people who purified themselves. Early scholars read the reply two ways: a straight path leading to Me, or a path binding upon Me. The sources keep both. What follows sets the limit precisely. There is no authority over God's servants, only over those who follow of their own accord. That reduces the earlier boast to an invitation nobody has to accept.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, completing the exchange that began with the making of the human being. The surah is addressing an audience under pressure from mockery and social cost. This passage tells them where the actual limits of that pressure lie. The scene is told in several surahs. This version is unusual for stating the number of gates in the closing verse.

keyTerms.note: From the root for separating a thing from what is mixed with it. The form here is passive, so purity is described as done to them. Early scholars note the difference from the active form.
The word for both political power and the warrant that authorises a claim. Denying it means no power to compel, which leaves only suggestion. The Quran elsewhere has this admitted openly.
From the root used two verses earlier, when he claimed he had been led astray himself. Repeating it makes his followers people in the same condition he described, rather than recruits he created.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Authority in Arabia was concrete and had to be backed. A man's word carried only as far as his clan could enforce it, and a claim without that backing was recognised for what it was. Everyone understood the difference between someone who could compel you and someone who could only call to you. The word denied here is the one that marks that line exactly.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran preserves a scene in which this claim is retracted in the plainest terms, with the same word. When the matter is settled, the one who made the boast tells his followers he had no authority over them at all. He says only that he called and they answered. He tells them to blame themselves rather than him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established that a reader under pressure needs to hold together. The reach of temptation is real, and it is limited to persuasion, since compulsion is ruled out here in words. The passive form of the word for the protected group matters just as much. It places their sincerity as something given rather than achieved. That removes any ground for feeling safe, while leaving the protection genuine.

crossReferences.why: Records the full retraction later, with the same word for authority denied outright.
States the same protection over God's servants and calls Him a sufficient guardian.
Gives the same boast and the same exception in a different surah, in an oath.

studies.applyIt: Think about how a bad choice actually arrived last time. It was probably not a force you could not resist. It was a suggestion that seemed reasonable at the moment. Name the last one in a sentence. Recognising it as a suggestion rather than a compulsion is the whole content of the limit stated here.
studies.explainEasier: Satan says he will lead people off the path, except the ones God has made pure. God answers that Satan has no power over his servants. He can only reach people who choose to follow him.

studies.title: Brothers On Facing Couches
studies.meaning: The description is built from removals as much as from gifts. Gardens and springs are named, then entry in peace and safety, and then the striking clause: whatever ill feeling was in their chests is drawn out. Early scholars take this as the removal of grudges carried from this life, so that people who had reason to resent each other sit facing one another as kin. Fatigue is denied, and being sent away is denied. The passage closes with an instruction to inform God's servants of two of His names.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage answers the section immediately before it, in which Satan is granted power only over those who follow him and Hell is described with seven gates. This is the counterweight, given in the same measured tone. No particular occasion is reported. The surah belongs to the middle Meccan years, when the small community was under social pressure and the promise of a place where no one can be expelled had a sharp edge.

keyTerms.note: The word names a hidden grudge lodged in the chest, not open hostility. The root is used of a hand bound to the neck, which gives the sense of something knotted and held rather than expressed.

A verb of pulling something out by force, used of drawing a bucket from a well or a weapon from its sheath. The grudges are extracted rather than forgotten, which implies they were real and lodged deep.

Bodily exhaustion from effort, distinct from grief or boredom. Denying it addresses a specific fear about eternity, that even rest becomes wearying, and the second denial answers the other fear, of being sent away.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Feuds in Arabia were handed down like property. A killing in one generation bound the next to answer it. Clans could carry a grievance for decades, reciting the names of the dead in poetry so no one forgot. Sitting face to face was a posture of trust, which is why guests were seated in view of each other. To promise that the grudges themselves would be pulled out was to promise something no truce had ever managed.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about drawing rancour from the chest occurs twice in the Quran. It is here, and in a passage on the people of the garden in another surah, with almost the same wording. The closing ayat also pair a name of forgiveness with a warning about punishment. The warning comes in the very next line. Early scholars treat that balance as a mark of this surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Paradise is described as a mending of relationships, not only as a reward. Something is taken out of the people themselves before they are seated together. That says the block to peace was inside them, and that God deals with it directly. The passage then turns from description to address. It orders that the servants be told what God is. The naming arrives as news to be carried. It is not a conclusion the hearer has to reach alone.

crossReferences.why: The same removal of rancour, there followed by the words of those who arrive.
A prayer of later believers asking that no rancour toward earlier ones remain in their hearts.
Also denies fatigue in the garden, in the words of those already inside it.

studies.applyIt: Bring to mind one person you have not forgiven. You do not have to contact them, and you do not have to feel differently. Just try, once, to describe what happened without the word they in an accusing position. Notice how hard that is. This passage says the grudge is something removed rather than argued away, and noticing its weight is where that begins.
studies.explainEasier: Good people will live in gardens with springs of water. God will take away any bad feeling they carried for each other. They will sit together like family. They will never get tired and never be sent away.

studies.title: The Guests Of Abraham
studies.meaning: Visitors arrive, offer peace, and the host answers that he is wary of them. The Arabic word for guest stays the same for one visitor or several, so the number is carried only by the verbs around it. Their reply comes in two parts. First it removes the fear, then it delivers good news of a boy who will have knowledge. Early scholars mostly identify him as Isaac, following another surah that names him outright. The sources record a minority reading.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This episode is told in at least four surahs with different details preserved. One gives the roasted calf brought out and untouched, which is what alarmed the host. Another records his wife's reaction. This surah omits the meal entirely and gives only the fear and the announcement. What it needs next is the errand these visitors are on.

keyTerms.note: A collective noun that does not change form between one visitor and many, so Arabic carries the number in the verbs alone. The same word will describe Lot's visitors a few verses later.
A quiet fear that unsettles rather than terrifies. The Quran uses the same root for hearts that tremble at the mention of God. So the word covers awe and alarm without separating them.
The second word is an intensive form, promising not merely a child but one who will know. What is announced is therefore a character rather than only an heir. That is unusual in such an announcement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hospitality in the desert was close to law. A stranger at your tent was fed before he was questioned. Refusing food was the known signal that a visit was not ordinary. That is why another telling of this story has the host grow suspicious when their hands did not reach toward the calf. Sharing food created a duty. Declining it declined the duty.
studies.didYouKnow: Abraham is named in the Quran more often than any prophet except Moses. He appears in some fifty verses across many surahs. The announcement of a son in old age recurs in several of these accounts. A comparable exchange is recorded for another prophet, who asks how he can have a son when old age has overtaken him and his wife is barren.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Good news arrives here inside an encounter that felt threatening. That is the structure of the passage rather than a moral drawn from it. The visitors' first task is to remove the fear, before anything is delivered. The announcement follows only after that. There is also a quiet claim in what is promised. The value named is knowledge rather than lineage, which is not what a man in that culture would have expected to hear.

crossReferences.why: Gives the fuller version with the untouched calf and names the son and his son after him.
Tells the same visit, records the wife's reaction, and uses the same phrase for a knowing boy.
States the errand the visitors are on, which this surah reveals only in the following verses.

studies.applyIt: Think of a piece of news that turned out well but arrived in a way that frightened you. A phone call at the wrong hour, an unexpected meeting. Notice that the fear and the news were separate things, and that one passed. Then let that shape how you handle the next unexpected knock, before you know what it is.
studies.explainEasier: Some visitors came to Abraham and said peace. He was uneasy about them. They told him not to be afraid. Then they gave him good news: he would have a son who would know a great deal.

studies.title: Who Despairs Of His Lord
studies.meaning: The question is not doubt but astonishment. It asks how such news can be brought to a man whom old age has already reached. The visitors answer that they bring it in truth. They tell him not to be among those who give up hope. His reply turns the instruction into a principle and hands it back. Who despairs of his Lord's mercy except those who have lost the way. Early scholars note that he does not deny having been startled. He denies that surprise and despair are the same thing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the middle of the account of Abraham's visitors. The exchange is preserved in several surahs, and in each one the reaction to the announcement is recorded rather than smoothed over. The audience for this surah was a community whose situation had not improved for years. The principle stated here arrives inside a story about news that came very late.

keyTerms.note: From the root for greatness and increase, so age is described as gathering rather than decline. The verb attached says it touched him, which makes it something that arrived rather than something he became.

Despair that follows expectation, distinct from the word for never having hoped at all. The Quran uses this root in its best-known verse against despair, addressed to those who have wronged themselves.

keyTerms.gloss: those who have lost the way
keyTerms.note: From the verb for losing a road or losing an object. Naming despair as a form of being lost makes it a navigation error. It is a wrong estimate of where things stand, rather than a mood.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Children were a household's only security in old age. A man without sons had nobody obliged to keep him, and there was no institution that would. The announcement in this story is therefore not sentimental. It addresses the most practical worry an ageing man in that world could carry. His startled question is the response of someone who had long since finished arranging his expectations.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses two different roots for despair and keeps them apart. One appears here, and in the verse telling those who have wronged themselves not to despair of God's mercy. The other is used by Jacob, when he tells his sons not to give up on God's relief. Both are placed in the mouths of prophets. Each is spoken to people who had reason to give up.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Despair is treated as a mistake about God, not as a feeling about your situation. That is why the answer is a question about who despairs. It is not a promise about what will happen. The reading holds however bad things are. What is wrong is the guess about what is still possible. The passage lets surprise stand. It only refuses the conclusion people usually draw from it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same root in the best-known verse against despair, addressed to those who transgressed.
Has Jacob use the other root for despair, telling his sons not to give up on God's relief.
Records a comparable question about a son in old age, asked by another prophet.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you have quietly written off. Not something you decided against; something you concluded was too late. Say to yourself only that you do not actually know that. You are not required to expect it. The passage treats despair as a claim about what is possible, and claims like that need evidence.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham was amazed. He asked how he could have a son when he was already old. The visitors said the news was true. They told him not to give up hope. He said only lost people give up on God.

studies.title: We Will Save Them All
studies.meaning: The visitors state their errand plainly and then begin narrowing it. Sent to a guilty people, except the household of Lot, whom they will deliver entirely. Except his wife, about whom a decision has already been made. Early scholars note the word used for her, which describes someone who stays behind rather than someone struck down. They read it as her belonging with the town rather than with the household. Then the scene shifts. The same visitors arrive at a door where they are not recognised.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This account appears in several surahs, and the exceptions are consistent across all of them. The Quran refers elsewhere to the wife of this prophet as an example of someone married into a righteous household who did not share its position. This surah gives the sequence compactly, moving from Abraham's tent to Lot's door in a single verse.

keyTerms.note: From a root for cutting or severing, used of picking fruit and of committing an offence. It names those who have broken off from what they owed. That is why the Quran applies it to whole communities.

The word for a person's family and immediate following, wider than blood. Using it here lets the deliverance cover a household rather than a bloodline. That is why the exception must be stated separately.
From a root for what stays after the rest has gone, used of dust settling. It describes her by position rather than by verdict. That is how the Quran consistently words this exception.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A household in that world meant everyone under a man's protection: wives, children, dependants and sometimes servants. They moved together. When a family left a town by night it left as a unit, and anyone who stayed had chosen the town over the household. That is the ordinary social fact behind the exception. Its first hearers would have understood it in exactly those terms.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran mentions two wives of prophets together as examples in a later surah. It says they were under two righteous servants and did not benefit from that in any way. The point made there is that being close confers nothing. This surah's account makes the same point by its structure, naming the household first and then removing one member from it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Deliverance is described as thorough and precisely bounded at the same time. The whole household is to be saved, which is emphatic. The single exception is stated in the same breath, which stops the promise being read as protection by association. What decides the outcome is where a person actually stands, not who they live with. The passage makes that point without any comment on it at all.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same exchange and the same exception, and adds the distress at their arrival.
Names two wives of prophets as examples of people who gained nothing from proximity.
Records the same errand in the visitors' own words, with the stones marked for the excessive.

studies.applyIt: Consider what you assume you have inherited spiritually from the people around you: a family reputation, a community, someone whose practice you admire. All of that is genuinely good. Then ask what you would still be standing on if none of it were there. Nobody in this account is saved by whose household they belong to.
studies.explainEasier: The visitors say they were sent to a guilty people. They will save Lot and everyone in his house. Only his wife is left out. She stays behind with the town.

studies.title: Travel While It Is Dark
studies.meaning: The visitors identify themselves by what they carry: the thing the town kept disputing. Then instructions arrive in a strict order. Move your household while the night is still deep. Follow at the rear of them. Let none of you turn to look, and go where you are told. Early scholars note that each instruction is practical. The one about looking back is the only one whose purpose is not stated. The final phrase leaves the destination unnamed, so the household is directed without being informed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The account appears in several surahs, and the night departure is constant across them. Another version records the visitors adding that the appointed time is the morning, and asking whether the morning is not near. This surah keeps the instructions and omits the reassurance. That leaves the passage sounding as urgent as the situation was.

keyTerms.note: From a root for pulling at something from two sides, as in milking or wrangling. It describes a doubt kept alive by argument, rather than one waiting to be settled by evidence.

A single verb meaning to journey in darkness, with no separate word for night required. The same verb is used for the night journey of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) at the opening of another surah.
The verb for twisting the head to glance behind, not merely for seeing. What is forbidden is the movement of turning, which is what slows a person and divides their attention on a night march.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night travel was standard practice in that climate, and everyone knew its discipline. You moved in the cool hours and kept the group tight. The one who knew the route walked where he could see everybody. Stragglers were the danger, and a family moving in darkness kept a man at the rear so that nobody was lost. The instructions here are the ordinary technique of a night departure.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to move by night is given to more than one prophet in the Quran, using the same verb. Moses receives it when he is told to take the servants of God out by night, because they will be pursued. The verb also opens the surah that describes the night journey. So a single word carries deliverance, escape and ascent across three different accounts.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance here arrives as a sequence of instructions with the destination withheld. That is a specific model of how following works. The household is told enough to move and not enough to plan. Obedience is measured by whether they keep going rather than by whether they understand. The ban on looking back is the sharpest part. What is asked is not only forward movement but the surrender of the urge to check what is being left.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instructions and adds that the appointed time for the town is the morning.
Uses the same verb for a night departure, given to Moses with the warning of pursuit.
Repeats that instruction in another surah, in the same compressed form.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you left behind that you keep revisiting in your mind: a city, a job, a version of yourself. Notice how much of this week's attention went backwards. Set one specific limit on it, such as not raising it in conversation for seven days. Then see what the forward attention does with the room.
studies.explainEasier: The visitors tell Lot to leave with his family while it is still dark. He must walk behind them. No one is allowed to turn and look back. They must keep going to the place they are told.

studies.title: These Are My Guests
studies.meaning: The decree is delivered, and then the townspeople arrive at the door in a mood the text calls delighted. Lot's appeal is made on three grounds in quick succession. These are my guests, do not expose me, be wary of God, do not disgrace me. Early scholars note that he argues from the duty of hospitality before anything else. In that setting it was the strongest claim available. The reply reveals the history: a standing instruction that he was not to shelter outsiders at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran tells this account in several surahs, and this version is the most compressed, keeping only the confrontation at the door. Its audience in Mecca included people sheltering vulnerable believers, sometimes against pressure from their own clans. A scene about a host defending guests would not have read as remote history to them.

keyTerms.note: From the root for good news and for skin, since news shows first in the face. Its use here is deliberately jarring, describing the arrival of a crowd in the language of glad tidings.
To uncover something that should stay covered, so the disgrace is specifically public. A host who could not protect a guest lost standing permanently. That is the injury being named.
The general word for creation and those who live in it, used here for outsiders. The phrasing shows the standing ban had been broad, covering strangers as a category rather than particular visitors.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Guarding a guest was the strongest duty in Arabian custom. In practice it was stronger than most claims of family. A man who took in a stranger became answerable for him. If he failed, poems recalled it for generations. Turning travellers away was not merely unkind in that world. It broke the whole arrangement that made travel possible, and towns known for it were avoided.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran records this town's practices in several places, and describes the visitors' arrival differently each time. One version says the host was distressed and called it a dreadful day. Another says the envoys were mistreated and told him not to fear or grieve. This surah alone records the townspeople's own reply, revealing a standing ban on his hosting anyone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A man under threat makes his appeal on ground everyone in the scene already accepts, and it fails. That failure is what the passage is documenting. It shows a community that had abandoned the most basic protection owed to a stranger. Placing the call to be wary of God between two appeals about shame is also deliberate. It shows him reaching past social pressure to something the crowd no longer felt.

crossReferences.why: Gives the fuller confrontation, with the host calling it a dreadful day and asking for one reasonable man.
Records the same arrival from the visitors' side, telling him not to fear or grieve.
States the outcome of the demand made at the door in the briefest terms.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone in your circle who is currently a guest in a broad sense: new, dependent, without standing of their own. A colleague on their first week, a relative staying with you, a newcomer at the mosque. Do one specific thing this week that costs you something to make their position easier.
studies.explainEasier: The men of the town came to Lot's door, pleased with themselves. He begged them to leave his guests alone. He told them to fear God, and not to shame him. They said he had been told to take in no one.

studies.title: Signs For Those Who Read Marks
studies.meaning: The host makes one last offer. Early scholars differ on what he meant. Some say the daughters were his own, offered in marriage. Others say a prophet is a father to his people, so the women of the town are meant. Then comes an oath, sworn on the life of the one addressed. The verdict follows: they were blundering in their drunkenness. The Blast comes at sunrise. The town is turned over, and stones of baked clay fall. The passage closes by saying there are signs here for those who can read marks.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the account of Lot's town. The sites tied to these events lay along the trade route north from Mecca toward Syria, which is why the next verse says the place is on a road still in use. The audience travelled that road, and the Quran repeatedly directs their attention to what they were passing without looking at.

keyTerms.note: An oath sworn on the life of the one addressed. It occurs once in the Quran, and the classical scholars read it as a mark of honour, since God swears here by the life of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).
From the root for being drunk or blocked, the same used earlier in this surah for eyes that seem stopped up. Early scholars take it here as a daze of desire rather than of wine.
Occurring once in the Quran, from a root for a brand or distinguishing mark. It names people who infer from traces, the skill of a tracker applied to the evidence of history.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tracking was a specialist art in Arabia. A skilled reader could tell from prints how many had passed, whether the camels were laden, how long ago they went and sometimes whose they were. Whole disputes were settled on such testimony. The word closing this passage borrows that expertise exactly, and asks for it to be turned on ruins rather than on footprints.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where an oath is sworn by the life of the one being addressed. The early scholars treat it as an honour given to no one else. The word for those who read marks is also unique to this verse. So two words found nowhere else in the Book sit within four verses of each other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Evidence here calls for a skill. That is not the same as calling for belief. The ruins stand where anyone can see them. Only those trained to read traces take anything from them. So attention is learned, not merely willed. That is why the Quran keeps telling people to travel and look. The oath in the middle does quiet work too. It treats the daze described as a real impairment, not as an excuse.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same offer and records the townspeople's reply, which this surah leaves out.
Describes the same destruction at dawn and the rescue of the household before it.
Names the stones of clay in the envoys' own words, before they reach the town.

studies.applyIt: Learn to read one set of traces you currently walk past. The age of a building on your street, what a tree's shape says about wind, why a road bends where it does. Ask someone or look it up. The closing word here names a skill, and skills are acquired by practising on something small.
studies.explainEasier: The man at the door makes one last offer. The crowd is too far gone to hear it. At sunrise a great blast hits the town. It is turned over and stones of baked clay fall. What is left is a sign to read.

studies.title: On A Road Still In Use
studies.meaning: The site of the last account is placed on the map. It lies on a road that is still there, and in that is a sign for those who believe. Then three short verses name two more peoples. The dwellers of the thicket did wrong, and payback followed. Both places, early scholars say, stand on a plain highway, or are kept in a clear record, since the phrase carries both senses. The last verse names the people this surah is titled after. They rejected the messengers sent to them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The northern trade route from Mecca toward Syria passed the settlements this passage names, and merchants covered it every season. Another surah tells its audience directly that they pass these places morning and evening. The argument depends on that geography: what is being pointed at was not remote, and the audience could have stopped and looked.

keyTerms.note: A route still standing and in use rather than a forgotten track. The second word means what remains established, so the phrase insists the evidence is current and not confined to memory.
Dense interlaced trees, which in that landscape marked a place with water. The people named after it appear in four surahs, always among the communities that rejected their messenger.

keyTerms.gloss: a clear road, a plain register
keyTerms.note: The word can mean a leader, a route followed, or a written record kept for reference. The classical scholars keep the whole range, and the ayah works under either reading.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravan routes were fixed by water rather than by preference. The northern road ran between known wells, and every stage was named and familiar to the men who worked it. Passing a ruined settlement was routine, and the guides could usually say whose it had been. The claim that a destroyed town lies on a road still in use was not a figure of speech; it was an item on the itinerary.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah is named after the people in its eightieth verse. That is the only place in the Quran where they are named in this way. The dwellers of the thicket turn up in four surahs. Each time they are listed among peoples who turned their messenger down. One passage groups them with the peoples named here, as allies in the same refusal.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grounds a moral claim in geography, which is a specific kind of argument. It does not ask the reader to accept a story on authority; it says the evidence stands on a road you use. That places the burden on attention rather than on trust. Naming several peoples in sequence also makes the point that this is a pattern, and patterns are the kind of thing that can be checked.

crossReferences.why: Tells the audience directly that they pass these places in the morning and at night.
Names the dwellers of the thicket and the messenger sent to them.
Groups these same peoples together as confederates in rejecting their messengers.

studies.applyIt: Find out what stood where you live before the buildings that are there now. A council archive, an old map, a neighbour who remembers. This passage says the evidence sits on a road you already use. The point is not old history. It is the habit of looking at what you pass each day.
studies.explainEasier: The ruined town from the last verses sits beside a road people still use. Two more peoples did wrong and were paid back for it. One of them is the people this chapter is named after. They turned their messengers away.

studies.title: Houses Carved In The Mountains
studies.meaning: Four short verses move from signs given to security assumed to the outcome. They received the signs and turned from them; they used to carve dwellings out of the rock, feeling safe; the Blast took them in the morning; what they had acquired was of no use. Early scholars note the word for feeling secure, which describes a state of mind rather than a fact about the stone. The last verse does not say their work was destroyed. It says it did not help.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The rock-cut facades north of Medina were visible from the trade road and were known to the audience by reputation. Another surah records that this people were told to remember being settled in the land, building mansions on the plains and carving dwellings in the mountains. The Quran refers to them repeatedly without ever needing to describe the site.

keyTerms.note: The verb for cutting a shape out of solid material, used of stone and wood. The tense describes a settled practice rather than a single project, so the carving was what these people were known for.
A state of mind rather than a fact about the structure. The root is the one behind faith and trustworthiness, so the word quietly notes where their confidence had been placed.
One shout or sudden sound. The Quran uses it for several destructions, and its force lies in the contrast between an enormous outcome and an instrument that leaves nothing to resist.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Stone building was rare in Arabia and cost a huge amount of labour. Most people lived in tents, palm-branch huts or mud brick. All of those needed repair again and again. Cutting a house out of a cliff said the family meant to stay for good. Travellers who passed those fronts were looking at the most lasting thing built in that landscape.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah is named after these people. The phrase that names them appears only in its eightieth verse. Elsewhere the Quran calls them by their tribal name. One passage describes them as those who carved the rocks in the valley. Another says they were guided but chose blindness over guidance. That is the same order of events this surah gives in short form.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The building is not what is faulted. The feeling that came with it is. A sense of safety attaches to whatever looks most lasting, and stone is the obvious choice. The last verse puts it exactly. What they had gained was real, and it did not help them. That is not the same as calling it worthless. A thing can be solid and still be the wrong thing to lean on.

crossReferences.why: Recalls the same practice, mansions on the plains and dwellings carved in the mountains.
Names the same people as those who carved the rocks in the valley.
Says they were guided but preferred blindness, and names the punishment that seized them.

studies.applyIt: Identify the thing that makes you feel safest: a savings figure, a qualification, a house that is nearly paid off. Do not disparage it, since the passage does not. Just ask what it actually protects against and what it does not, and say both answers out loud. The security in this account was a feeling, not a survey of the stone.
studies.explainEasier: These people were given clear signs and turned away from them. They cut their homes right out of the rock and felt safe there. Then a blast hit them one morning. All the work they had done did not save them.

studies.title: Overlook With Gracious Overlooking
studies.meaning: Three statements, with the instruction set in the middle of them. Nothing was made except with truth. The Hour is coming, so turn away kindly. Early scholars read that phrase as pardon with no rebuke attached. Nothing is said about it afterwards, and no score is kept. Then comes a name for God that joins constant making with full knowing. Last comes a reminder of what has already been given: seven of the oft-repeated, and the Grand Quran. Most classical readings take the seven as the opening surah. The sources also keep a view that they are the long surahs.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken to a man taking daily hostility in a city he could not leave. The order to overlook belongs to this period. Other passages give the same guidance in different words. One adds that it should go on until God brings his command. Nothing here reports a single incident. It speaks to the standing situation.

keyTerms.note: The noun means turning the side or the page, and the adjective means beautiful. Together the early scholars read them as pardon without rebuke, so nothing is said afterwards about what was overlooked.
An intensive form describing creation as ongoing practice rather than a completed act. It occurs twice in the Quran, and both times it is paired with the name for complete knowledge.
From a root for doubling and repeating. Most early scholars take the seven as the verses of the opening surah, repeated in every prayer, and the sources also keep a reading of the seven long surahs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grievances in Arabia were kept and recited. A wrong was remembered, named in poetry, and brought out years later when it became useful. Forgiving in public while still mentioning it was normal. What this instruction asks for cut against all of that. Turning away with no comment meant giving up the one payment an injured party was always allowed to keep.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for gracious turning away occurs once in the Quran with this exact wording. The phrase naming what has been given, seven of the oft-repeated, also occurs only here. That is why the classical scholars discuss what it means at such length. Two phrases unique to the Book sit within three verses of one another.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgiveness rests on two facts stated before it, not on what the wrongdoer deserves. Creation has a purpose, and the Hour is coming. So nothing is dropped here. It is handed on. That makes overlooking a form of trust rather than a loss. The reminder of what has been given finishes the reasoning. A man who holds the opening of this Book in every prayer has been paid in advance for what he is asked to let go.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction to pardon and overlook, until God brings His command.
Repeats it in a different form, to pardon and say peace, since they will come to know.
States the same ground, that the heavens and earth were not created in play.

studies.applyIt: Pick one grievance small enough to actually let go of, and let it go completely. That means not mentioning it, not alluding to it, and not saving it for an argument later. Most of us forgive while keeping the receipt. The phrase here is specifically about the receipt.
studies.explainEasier: God made the sky and the earth for a reason, and a day is coming when it all gets settled. So let people off kindly and do not bring it up again. You have been given more than you are giving up.

studies.title: Do Not Stretch Your Eyes
studies.meaning: Three instructions in one breath. Each one answers a different pressure. The first forbids a lingering look at the comfort given to groups among the opponents. The verb suggests stretching the gaze, not glancing. The second forbids grief over them. Early scholars read that as sorrow at their refusal, not at their wealth. The third asks for gentleness towards believers. It uses the image of a bird lowering its wing over its young.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, late in the period there. The ayah comes straight after the mention of the seven oft-repeated verses and the Grand Quran. The order is deliberate: you have been given this, so do not look at that. Opponents in Mecca included some of the richest families in the city. The small group around the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) came mostly from people with no such backing. No occasion is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of extending a rope or a shadow. Applied to the eyes it describes a look that keeps going, so what is discouraged is dwelling rather than seeing.
An intensive form of a verb meaning to furnish with goods for a time. The word itself carries a term limit, so the very phrase describing their wealth marks it as temporary.
A bird lowers its wing to shelter its young and raises it to threaten. The idiom means to make yourself approachable and safe, and the same image appears in the command about ageing parents.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Mecca showed in a few specific things. The number of camels in a caravan share. A house near the sanctuary. Clients who owed you. Daughters married into other clans. There was no way not to notice who had them. The believers included freed slaves and men who had been cast off by their families.
